newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian Nobel laureate renews protest at TV law.
newsitem.headline: Colombian Nobel laureate renews protest at TV law.

text.p: Colombian Nobel laureate Gabriel Garcia Marquez said on Thursday the government was planning to play political favorites in its shake-up of television programming later this year.
Garcia Marquez said he would sell his shareholding in the QAP TV news show in protest at the new law, which obliges program-makers to submit new bids for broadcast slots.

Opponents of the law fear it will be used to punish those news shows that were most critical of President Ernesto Samper during the scandal over allegations that Samper funded his 1994 campaign with drug money.

"We think this government will not offer the minimum conditions of equity, nor do we recognize the National Television Commission (CNTV) as having sufficient autonomy to guarantee a selection process free from prejudice or political favoritism," the world-famous author said in a statement co-signed by Enrique Santos, deputy editor of the leading El Tiempo newspaper.
Santos also has a major shareholding in QAP.

Samper has repeatedly said the new contracts would be awarded fairly on the basis of the professionalism of the bidders. He has said the law would help make television more "democratic" by allowing for the creation of two private national TV channels, in addition to the existing three state-operated channels.
Under the terms of the new TV law, approved by the constitutional court last month, new broadcast contracts will be awarded in October and the new program schedule will begin in January.
Critics say the CNTV, which will evaluate the bids, is packed with Samper's political cronies who will rid the airwaves of government critics in the run-up to the 1998 presidential elections.
Garcia Marquez previously said some aspects of the new law were "the most brutal form of censorship on freedom of thought."

Garcia Marquez, a prolific author of novels and short stories, was awarded the Nobel Prize for literature in 1982. His international fame sprang from the novel "100 Years of Solitude," which was first published in 1967 and became Latin America's most successful novel.
